answer:
Noise wears down entanglement, and it gets worse as more qubits are entangled. In a perfect GHZ state, every shot reads all 0s or all 1s. On the real sirius QPU, the share of shots where all bits agreed was 95% for 2 qubits, 89% for 3, 81% for 4, and 72% for 5.

What I ran: I built four GHZ circuits with 2, 3, 4, and 5 qubits and sent them as one job with 100 shots per circuit. Each circuit puts the first qubit into a superposition with a Hadamard gate. A chain of CNOT gates then links each next qubit to the one before it. A perfect machine would give about half all-0s and half all-1s, so the ideal agreement is 100% at every size. I tested the same job on the free sirius:mock device first (job 01a16052-3864-732e-a29e-a5ca69fc92e2). The mock completed without errors, but its counts are not real physics. It returned all 0s every time. Then I ran the one authorized real job on sirius (job 01a16052-780d-726a-92db-c79833336824). The API reports 1.0 billed second for it. At 0.3 credits per second, that is about 0.3 credits.

Why agreement drops: Sirius has a star layout. Each qubit talks to the others through a central resonator, so every entangling step needs MOVE operations as well as a CZ gate. The 2-qubit circuit used 1 CZ and 2 MOVEs. The 5-qubit circuit used 4 CZs and 8 MOVEs. Each extra qubit adds gates, and every gate has a small chance of error. Each extra qubit also adds one more readout that can flip by mistake. One error anywhere is enough to break the all-agree pattern. The losses add up, so agreement fell by about 6 to 9 points per added qubit.

Limits: with 100 shots, each fraction has an uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 3 to 5 points. The downward trend is still clear.

The principle: entangled states are fragile. A larger entangled state has more places where noise can get in, so its quality falls quickly as it grows. This is the reason real quantum computers need error mitigation and, in the end, error correction.
